newsitem.title: UK: British firms join foreign income dividend rush.
newsitem.headline: British firms join foreign income dividend rush.

text.p: Recent tax changes will send more British companies scrambling to pay foreign income dividends (Fids) before they are scrapped in April 1999, tax experts said on Friday.
"There are quite a few companies that have paid Fids in the past. I would expect there will be a lot more now," Richard Law, tax partner at accountants Ernst & Young told Reuters.
Earlier international chemicals group Courtaulds Plc joined British drinks group Allied Domecq Plc in switching dividend payments to Fids.
Courtaulds said it would pay its final dividend as a Fid, citing a saving of 12.0 million pounds ($20.2 million) as the reasoning for the change. The move must be approved by shareholders at its AGM.

While this is a short term answer to rule changes on advanced corporation tax (ACT), it leaves open the question of what British firms with high levels of foreign income will do if Fids are abolished.

Over the last week there has been intense pressure on the government to retreat on its budget pledge to abolish the dividends, with mutterings from some quarters that companies will relocate rather than face paying tax twice.
But whatever the final outcome, if companies opt for foreign income dividend payments in the interim, it could have serious ramifications for the government's grip on its purse strings.
"If everyone does go for a Fid, they could end up losing a lot of income," one tax expert said. The companies most likely to take this approach are those with overseas subsidiaries.
Courtaulds said a substantial proportion of its profits were earned and taxed overseas and in the past the ACT it has had to pay on its dividends has exceeded corporation tax payable in Britain.
As a result it now has carried forward surplus ACT, written off but still available to the company, totalling some 42.0 million pounds.
The threat of Fids being abolished has prompted it to take a cash flow benefit and reduce its exposure to the risk that its surplus ACT may not be recovered.

Other companies with significant foreign income are also likely to follow this line of thinking, fearful the surplus ACT they had built up over the years might not be absorbed by future British income.
Allied Domecq has already said it will pay its interim dividend as a Fid, which will enable it to obtain a refund of 25 million pounds.
Despite the pressure for change, and suggestions in British newspapers that the government would announce a climbdown from its initial plan, the government has not yet shifted.
On Thursday Chief Secretary to the Treasury Alistair Darling said there would be no reversal of last week's budget decision, although the government is discussing ways of softening the blow.
A number of large firms have already said they are keeping their options open over the proposals.
Rio Tinto Plc, the London-based resources group, said it was studying the detailed implications of the proposals but that it was concerned about the planned abolition of Fids in April 1999.
Suggestions companies would move offshore were also dismissed by Darling.
"You have to be careful about companies who say, 'if something happens, then we'll leave the country'. They tend not to do that," he said.

Fids were introduced in 1993 by the then Conservative government to preclude double taxation of dividends. They allow companies to avoid paying British advanced corporation tax on distributed earnings that have already been taxed abroad.
